course_description:
The course provides an introduction to composite materials, manufacturing and design with a primary focus on applications in the aerospace industry. Students will gain insight into the commonly used constituent materials, intermediates, and resulting composites and understand the many choices available in this hierarchy. The course will then introduce the students to the most common composite manufacturing processes for both thermoplastic and thermosetting matrix composites. Emphasis is put on enabling students to select the most appropriate manufacturing process for a given application and material combination. The design component of the course covers the key concepts of structural design and evaluation of composite materials. This includes introducing students to micromechanics, classical-laminate theory, and failure theory of composite materials using both analytical as well as numerical methods. In the final two weeks of the semester, the course ventures into advanced topics, including non-destructive testing, quality assurance, and ceramic matrix composite materials. The learning experience is enhanced through a hands-on manufacturing practical in which students work in teams, under the guidance of teaching staff, to manufacture aerospace-grade composite components.

Composite materials are one of the most important group of materials for lightweight aerospace applications and are now also rapidly gaining importance in a wide variety of other engineering applications. In contrast to more traditional engineering materials, composite materials offer a unique and large design space as constituent materials can be selected and orientated to address very specific performance requirements. This design freedom leads to an intimate connection between materials, manufacturing and design which can be challenging for engineers.

The purpose of this course is to develop your knowledge of these three important aspects of composite engineering (materials, manufacturing and design) and to teach an understanding of the connection between materials, manufacturing, and design.

The course provides an introduction to composite constituent materials, intermediate forms and engineering composites, with a primary focus on aerospace applications. Students develop an understanding of the hierarchy of composite materials and the many design choices available. The course then introduces the principal manufacturing processes for both thermoplastic and thermosetting composites, with emphasis on selecting the most appropriate manufacturing route for a given material system and application. The design component covers the fundamental principles of structural analysis and evaluation of composite materials, including micromechanics, Classical Laminate Theory, composite failure theories, and both analytical and numerical methods. The final part of the course explores advanced topics, including sandwich structures, degradation and durability, non-destructive testing, quality assurance, and ceramic matrix composites.

The course is centred around Project COMET (Composite Manufacturing, Engineering and Testbed) , which serves as a unifying platform integrating the theoretical and practical components of the course. Students apply composite analysis, structural design and manufacturing principles to a large fixed-wing UAV, providing a realistic aerospace engineering context that links materials selection, manufacturing, structural analysis and systems integration. The learning experience is further enhanced through hands-on manufacturing practicals, where student teams manufacture aerospace-grade composite components that are incorporated into the UAV, which is subsequently assembled, tested and evaluated as part of the course. Students also participate in a practical workshop on non-destructive testing and quality assurance, reinforcing the importance of manufacturing quality and structural integrity in aerospace composite structures.

The course will give students the necessary background knowledge to select composite materials for a specific application, determine suitable manufacturing options and to perform structural design and evaluation tasks. ﾠ

learning_outcomes.description: Select appropriate composite material systems to meet the requirements of specific applications.
Determine suitable manufacturing methods for composite materials based on application, cost, and performance considerations.
Apply composite mechanics and design principles to engineer composite structures.
Specify appropriate destructive and non-destructive testing methods for quality assurance during manufacturing and through-life support.

assessment_details.title: Materials and Manufacturing Poster
assessment_details.task_description: This assessment applies the knowledge and skills developed during the first part of the course (Materials and Manufacturing) to the design of the COMET (Composite Materials Engineering Testbed) unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV). This is an individual assessment. Each student will be assigned a specific UAV component group (e.g. wing structure, fuselage, control surfaces, propulsion integration or payload structure) and will evaluate suitable engineering materials, manufacturing processes and associated design considerations. Students are expected to justify their recommendations based on material properties, manufacturing capability, structural performance, cost, sustainability and other relevant engineering criteria. The findings are to be presented in the form of an engineering poster, summarising the design requirements, material selection process, manufacturing evaluation and the recommended engineering solution. The poster should communicate the information in a concise, visually effective and technically rigorous manner suitable for a professional engineering audience. A detailed introduction to the project will be provided during the studio in Week 2. This will include the marking criteria for the poster. It will also be made available on Blackboard. This task has been designed to be challenging, authentic and complex. Whilst students may use AI and/or MT technologies, successful completion of assessment in this course will require students to critically engage in specific contexts and tasks for which artificial intelligence will provide only limited support and guidance. A failure to reference generative AI or MT use may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct. To pass this assessment, students will be required to demonstrate detailed comprehension of their written submission independent of AI and MT tools. assessment_details.title: Workshop and NDT Studio participation assessment
assessment_details.task_description: This assessment evaluates the learning objectives associated with the workshop and NDT studio activities. The proposed assessment is marked out of 100 and is based on student participation and engagement in the hands-on components. 50 marks are available for the workshop component, and 50 marks are available for the NDT studio activities. A maximum of 100 marks may be awarded for the quality of participation. The proposed marking scale is as follows: · 0 marks – Non-attendance or disruptive behaviour. · 50 marks – Attendance with limited engagement or contribution to the activities. · 100 marks – Strong engagement, constructive participation, and active contribution throughout the practical activities. This assessment is intended to encourage active participation while recognising the importance of professional conduct, teamwork, and engagement in practical engineering activities.
